segments.original: Since the release of Jaws (1975), summer box office champions (or blockbusters) have been aimed at younger audiences. Epics and dramas for adults are a thing of the past: recent decades have been dominated by family entertainment. For the industry, this shift has meant increased profits that go beyond box office receipts, ranging from toys and other merchandise to sales of videos, DVDs, and Blu-rays, which often generate more revenue than the theatrical release itself.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Like the trilogy written by J. R. R. Tolkien, Peter Jackson's adaptation of The Lord of the Rings should be considered a single work, albeit a very long one. Seen in sequence, the three films form an almost perfect whole, from the spectacular prologue to the epic list of credits, a true record-breaker. Everything about this film is unprecedented in the history of cinema. The three parts were shot over a continuous period of 16 months. And the series' incredible popularity more than lived up to all expectations. It is estimated to have earned almost three billion dollars at the box office, more than any other trilogy, beating even the Star Wars blockbusters. According to some experts' estimates, DVD sales amount to at least the same figure, not to mention the exploitation of a line of licensed products, which means that Middle-earth's GDP rivals that of many real countries. Fortunately, Jackson managed to stun not only the accountants but also the critics. Each film outdid the previous one on best-of lists, and the three together racked up no fewer than 30 Oscar nominations, taking home 17 statuettes.

segments.original: If you have seen all three films, you won't be surprised to learn that they won the Oscar for visual effects. They are all packed with monsters and battles that become more impressive with each installment. Even so, it was the tragic figure of Gollum that managed to capture audiences' imagination. Based on movements stored in the computer and on the voice of actor Andy Serkis (b. 1964) — who would become a benchmark in motion capture and, a few years later, would play Caesar in the new Planet of the Apes trilogy (2011-2017) — the screen Gollum was entirely digital and yet as convincing as a flesh-and-blood character.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Perhaps that is Jackson's greatest achievement: remembering that cutting-edge special effects and technical mastery are not enough to make a great film. Although its leads are hobbits, elves, and wizards, all the characters are deeply human. Gollum has regrets, tries to be good, and taunts Sam, the "fat hobbit." The wizard Gandalf, played to perfection by Ian McKellen (b. 1939), is at times paternalistic and even mischievous, but never loses his aura of power and authority. And the hobbits Frodo (wide-eyed Elijah Wood) and Sam (Sean Astin) start out as brave but naive adventurers until they attain the status of true heroes. Almost as memorable as the characters is the setting. The trilogy was produced in Jackson's homeland, New Zealand, and very little digital magic was needed to create the dazzling landscapes. One of the most memorable scenes of the spectacular The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King (2003) is the lighting of the beacons as the music swells. The camera simply travels from one mountaintop to the next as the warning signal is lit and surges against the sky. Simply marvelous.

segments.original: It is also remarkable that Jackson and his co-writers Fran Walsh (b. 1959) and Philippa Boyens (b. 1962) managed to extract a gripping, fast-paced narrative from such a dense and seemingly impenetrable source. Even more remarkable is the fact that even the book's most hardcore fans loved the film. In the short, dramatic prologue, we learn that Sauron, the embodiment of evil, poured all his power into forging a ring, which was lost in an epic battle against an alliance of men and elves. The ring eventually ends up in the hands of the little hobbit Frodo Baggins. This is where the story begins. Frodo agrees to destroy it and thereby defeat Sauron once and for all. However, the ring can only be destroyed if it is cast into the volcanic heart of Mount Doom, which lies, of course, deep inside enemy territory. He sets out on this perilous journey in the company of a group of devoted hobbits, elves, dwarves, and men, including the wizard Gandalf and the mysterious Aragorn (Viggo Mortensen). Betrayal, bloodshed, and battles end up splitting the group, and Frodo, with Sam (and later with Gollum), sets off for the volcano alone, while the others prepare to stand against Sauron in a battle that will shake Middle-earth.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Despite the breadth of the canvas Jackson paints, the essence of his work is people, their relationships, and the decisions they must make. Friendship and self-sacrifice are strongly present, as is a sense of mortality. The final scenes make it clear that victory may be noble, yet may still come from an extremely painful personal sacrifice. Tolkien served in the trenches of World War I, and it is hard not to draw parallels between his experiences and the tone of melancholy that ultimately surrounds the final part of the trilogy. For many, the heart of the film lies not in the scenes of bravery but in a quiet moment in which Gandalf consoles Frodo, distraught at having to witness such terrible times. "So do all who live to see such times," says the wizard, "but that is not for them to decide. All we have to decide is what to do with the time that is given to us." It is moments like this that raise Jackson's film to the status of a masterpiece.

segments.original: Other dominant forces at the box office during this period were the revitalized comic book publishers DC and Marvel. With the success of X-Men (2000), Spider-Man (2002), and Iron Man (2008), Marvel was now able to finance its own productions, starting a trend that would dominate the box office over the next decade. segments.original: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban, as cinema, is one of the best in the series, because it represents a great leap forward from its predecessors. As an adaptation, however, it is somewhat disappointing because of the film's lack of fidelity to the work that gave rise to it. But since we know that literature and cinema are two completely different languages, let us analyze the film from a cinematic point of view.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Chris Columbus, director of the two previous adventures, this time takes on only the role of producer, worn out after so much work. So the Mexican director Alfonso Cuarón, best known for Y tu mamá también (2001), was called in to helm this third adventure. Right from the start, it was clear this would be a difficult job, since the third book is one of the most complex and challenging in the series, not only because of its more mature plot, but because it is here that the characters begin to deal more intensely with their teenage feelings. Fortunately, Cuarón overcame all these obstacles and created one of the best films in the series, more fun and darker. Despite working with the same crew as the previous films, Cuarón makes the production evolve in many respects, starting with the look. While in the first films the costumes, though creative, felt somewhat repetitive, the director made a wise choice in letting the leads wear their own clothes, and this choice works perfectly, since we feel the actors are more at ease in their roles. This gives the film a more modern look, as well as making it more relatable to most of its teenage fans.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: And if there is one thing Cuarón does well, it is putting his stamp on the film without making it feel "too auteurist." Using his camera more intensely than Columbus, the director opts for close-ups and creative movements, as well as wider shots that convey all the beauty and grandeur of the Hogwarts settings. The director emphasizes the empty, gloomy atmosphere of the landscapes, always overcast, which help create the ideal dark tone. Cuarón also gives the film a delightful pace, making it far less tedious than the first two. The customary opening at the Dursleys' house, for example, is quick, but it clearly defines what Potter is now: someone who is growing up, who is starting to take on teenage traits (notice how he is almost always irritated) — in short, he is beginning to mature.

segments.original: The new elements introduced also make the film much more appealing. This time, magical creatures appear in greater numbers, ranging from Hippogriffs (a kind of cross between a horse and an eagle), through a boggart, to the Dementors, beings that suck out people's souls. Once again, the film stands out for the number of well-known names from British film and theater. While Maggie Smith and Alan Rickman need no praise, there are some new additions, such as Michael Gambon, who replaces the late Richard Harris as Albus Dumbledore. Gambon brings a much more active air to the character, erasing the sluggish image Harris had built for the wizard. David Thewlis plays Remus Lupin with great warmth, while Gary Oldman delivers a fantastic portrayal of Sirius Black, the prisoner of the title.
